Benchmarking: cell calling and ambient RNA removal

2026-08-04

Run: 260528_VH01624_464_222K7VKNX / LK2-GEX. The comparison was carried out on LK2; CellBender was also run on LK1-resequenced.

Status: settled for the pipeline, which runs both emptyDrops and CellBender and records their overlap per run.

Analysis finished: 2026-06-29 - the most recent of the 17 figures shown below.

Report generated: 2026-08-04 by 07.cell_calling_report.Rmd, from the outputs of steps 01-06 in this folder.

Cell Ranger’s own cell calling is conservative and drops small cells, T-cells in particular. Two alternatives were tested: emptyDrops, which decides whether a droplet holds more structured RNA than the ambient profile predicts, and CellBender, which models the ambient contamination and subtracts it.

For full report, download cell_calling_report.html in the attachment and open in a browser.

Code used - attached and in the github repository: https://github.com/nbartonicek/surface_proteome_dev/tree/main/lab_archives/Benchmarking-cell_calling_and_ambient_RNA_removal

Aim

Decide which barcodes to carry forward as real cells, and how much ambient RNA to remove:

  • does emptyDrops recover the small cells Cell Ranger discards
  • does CellBender agree with emptyDrops on which barcodes are cells
  • what expected-cells and total-droplets-included should CellBender use
  • what do the barcodes the two methods disagree about actually look like

Conclusions

  • Cell Ranger is fairly conservative and eliminates small cells, T-cells in particular; emptyDrops recovers roughly 1,000 more cells on run 1 (24,334)
  • run 2 raises the opposite problem: emptyDrops calls fewer cells than Cell Ranger (31,198 against 32,846), and the extra barcodes are largely dead cells - so more calls is not automatically better
  • the working combination is emptyDrops plus CellBender with a mitochondrial cleanup, rather than either tool alone
  • MT cutoffs are taken from the literature rather than picked here: van Galen 20%, Petti 10%, Beneyto 20%, Zeng 20%
  • the fraction of counts removed stays under 5% in every configuration tried (2.3% to 4.3%), so CellBender is not stripping a large part of the signal
  • the droplet padding matters less than expected: +15,000 and +30,000 total droplets give substantially overlapping barcode sets, which is what the Venn diagrams below show
  • raising total-droplets-included raises found_cells (35,358 to 38,215 on LK2) while lowering the fraction removed, so the two settings trade off against each other rather than one dominating

1. emptyDrops

Step 01 runs DropletUtils::emptyDrops on the raw Cell Ranger matrix and keeps barcodes at FDR <= 0.01. It estimates the ambient RNA profile from the low-count droplets and then tests, per droplet, whether its content is more structured than that profile would produce. That is what lets it recover small cells a simple UMI-rank cutoff discards.

2. CellBender and the droplet sweep

CellBender 0.3.0 was run in a container (step 02). expected-cells is estimated from the data; total-droplets-included sets how far down the UMI rank the model looks for ambient signal. Two settings were tried:

Step total-droplets-included Output
02 expected + 15,000 cellbender/<run>/<sample>/
03 expected + 30,000 cellbender/<run>/<sample>_e30000/

Those are the 32k and 32k30k arms in the figure names below.

Four configurations were run in total, three of them on LK2. The numbers below are from the CellBender metrics of each run, as reported in the 2026-07-13 progress slides:

LK1 23k+15k LK2 33k+15k LK2 25k+15k LK2 33k+30k
expected_cells 23,569 32,846 25,000 32,846
found_cells 23,595 35,358 34,658 38,215
fraction_counts_removed 0.023 0.034 0.043 0.031

The diagnostic below is the panel to read: the black line is the UMI count per barcode in rank order, the red points are CellBender’s inferred cell probability. Where the red cloud breaks up is where the model stops being confident a droplet holds a cell.

cellbender_LK1_23k_15k.png

LK1, expected 23,569 + 15,000 droplets. 23,595 cells found, 2.3% of counts removed - the cleanest of the four, and the boundary is sharp.

cellbender_LK2_33k_15k.png

LK2, expected 32,846 + 15,000. 35,358 cells, 3.4% removed. The adopted setting (step 02).

cellbender_LK2_25k_15k.png

LK2, expected 25,000 + 15,000. 34,658 cells, 4.3% removed - understating expected-cells costs the most signal of the three.

cellbender_LK2_33k_30k.png

LK2, expected 32,846 + 30,000 (step 03). 38,215 cells, 3.1% removed. Widening the droplet window finds more cells and removes proportionally less.

6. What was run, in order

Step Script What it does
01 01.emptydrops.R emptyDrops on the raw matrix, FDR <= 0.01.
02 02.cellbender_run.sh CellBender 0.3.0 in a container, expected + 15,000 droplets.
03 03.cellbender_run_30k_droplets.sh The +30,000 droplet arm of the sweep.
04 04.cellbender_qc.R Post-CellBender QC: knee plot, UMI before/after, percent background removed.
05 05.compare_emptydrops_cellbender.R Barcode overlap, Venns at 25k and 32k, category breakdown.
06 06.compare_emptydrops_cellbender_extended.R Adds the +30k arm, four-way Venn, and per-category QC.
07 07.cell_calling_report.Rmd This report.

Two earlier attempts at the CellBender run are not kept: scripts/2a.cellbender.sh (2026-06-19, before containerisation) and scripts/2b.cellbender_docker.sh (2026-06-23, containerised but before the fix). Step 02 supersedes both.

Steps 05 and 06 are both kept, which is the exception to merging revisions into one step. They ran on different days and neither reproduces the other’s output: step 05 wrote the 25k and 32k Venns on 2026-06-24, step 06 wrote the 32k30k arm, the four-way Venn and the QC violins on 2026-06-29.

9. Caveats

  1. The full comparison exists for LK2 only. CellBender was also run on LK1-resequenced, but cellbender_comparison/ has just the one run, so the Venns and category QC are LK2’s.
  2. The cell counts in the conclusions come from the meeting slides, not from a saved summary table - 24,334 for run 1 and 31,198 against Cell Ranger’s 32,846 for run 2.
  3. MT cutoffs are literature values, listed for reference rather than derived here.
